children: Union Bank of India expects food inflation to accelerate to 7.35 per cent, driven by surging vegetable and onion prices, supply disruptions and below-average monsoon rainfall

India’s retail inflation is projected to rise to 5.47 per cent in September 2026 from 4.82 per cent in August, driven by a sharp increase in food prices, according to a report by Union Bank of India (UBI).
The projected increase would take headline inflation to its highest level since December 2024 and above the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) 4 per cent medium-term target, the report said.

Food inflation is estimated to have accelerated to 7.35 per cent in September from 5.66 per cent in August, with vegetables accounting for a significant share of the increase. Vegetable inflation is projected to jump to 9.34 per cent from 0.99 per cent a month earlier.

Onion prices rose by around 34 per cent during September, according to data from the Department of Consumer Affairs cited in the report. Inflationary pressures also extended to cereals, pulses, sugar, edible oils and milk.
Food Prices Face Weather And Supply Pressures
UBI attributed the expected increase in inflation to prolonged supply disruptions, higher energy costs, rising global chip prices and the potential effects of a strong El Niño weather phenomenon.

The southwest monsoon ended the June-September 2026 season with rainfall 13 per cent below the long-period average. Reservoir levels stood at 72 per cent, compared with 92 per cent a year earlier, potentially adding to agricultural supply pressures.
Total kharif crop sowing was around 1 per cent lower than the previous year, while paddy sowing declined by nearly 3 per cent.

The report noted that food inflation had risen from 2.12 per cent in January 2026 to 5.66 per cent in August, reflecting persistent price pressures despite a favourable base effect from the previous year.

Price pressures are expected to extend beyond food, with core inflation, which excludes more volatile components, projected to increase marginally to 4.48 per cent in September from 4.44 per cent in August.
The broad-based rise suggests that supply-side shocks and higher input costs are increasingly feeding into the wider inflation basket.

The inflation outlook will remain sensitive to food supply conditions, energy prices and weather developments in the coming months, as policymakers assess the implications for household purchasing power and monetary policy.
